questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests branchless bitwise selection across a 128-bit value. It mirrors practical use cases like compositing two 128-bit values with a mask in a single pass.

## Key Concepts

- Branchless bitwise selection
- 128-bit composition via hi/lo fields
- Handling of full-range masks across both lanes

## Code Example

```c
uint128 blend128(uint128 a, uint128 b, uint128 mask) {
  uint128 t1 = and128(a, mask);
  uint128 t2 = and128(b, not128(mask));
  return or128(t1, t2);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you validate correctness across all 2^128 mask patterns efficiently?
- How would this approach extend to 256-bit operands with the same interface?

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to engineer branchless, fixed-time bit-twiddling for 128-bit data—a common pattern in media and crypto pipelines where endianness and per-half constraints matter.

## Key Concepts
- **Cascaded byte-shuffling** using masks and shifts
- **In-half operations**: bytes never cross between the hi and lo 64-bit halves
- Endianness-aware byte-level manipulation

## When to Use This
This technique is essential in:
- Cryptography (byte-swap operations for AES, SHA)
- Network protocol implementations ( endianness conversion)
- Low-level systems programming where timing-constant operations matter

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to implement a rotation primitive with wrap-around using only shifts and masks, including masking to handle large r and the n=0 edge case.

## Key Concepts
- Circular shift using (x << n) | (x >> (32 - n))
- Masking r with 31 to confine to 0..31
- Edge-case n=0 preserves x exactly

## Code Example
```c
static inline uint32_t rotl32(uint32_t x, unsigned r) {
  unsigned n = r & 31; // 0..31
  return (x << n) | (x >> (32 - n));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you generalize to 64-bit rotates?
- What are the potential performance differences vs. compiler intrinsics like _rotl?
- How would you test across boundary values (r=0, r=31, r=32, r=33)?

## Why This Is Asked

This question tests precise bit-level reasoning and avoids expensive operations in tight loops, useful in storage engines and query optimizers.

## Key Concepts

- Single-set-bit test: (n & (n-1)) == 0
- Even-index bit mask: 0x55555555
- Combining tests with boolean logic for a robust check

## Code Example

```javascript
function isSingleEvenBitSet(n) {
  return n !== 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0 && (n & 0x55555555) !== 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you generalize to check exactly k bits set?
- How would you adapt to 64-bit width and different bit-ordering considerations?

## Why This Is Asked
Assesses pattern recognition and solid bit-twiddling under time pressure.

## Key Concepts
- Alternating bit patterns (0101..., 1010...)
- Using XOR with shifted version to collapse pattern
- Detecting all-ones masks with (x & (x+1)) == 0

## Code Example
```javascript
function hasAlternatingBits(n) {
  const x = (n ^ (n >>> 1)) >>> 0;
  return (x & (x + 1)) === 0;
}
```

- How to implement without using addition?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to implement a classic bit manipulation pattern without branches, reflecting real-world needs in low-level systems.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation vs shift
- Handling 32-bit wrap with modulo 32
- Edge case k=0 without branches

## Code Example
```javascript
uint32_t rotateLeft32(uint32_t n, unsigned int k) {
  k &= 31; // k % 32
  return (n << k) | (n >> (32 - k));
}
